d3dx9.lib — Microsoft D3DX9 import library, as game.dat links it
================================================================

d3dx9.lib
  sha256  b8e6e388d83849328cd291064b075369233f20153bc6ad575aaab557cd89241b
  size    87,226 bytes
  dated   2005-07-22
  from    DirectX 9.0c SDK (August 2005), Lib/x86/d3dx9.lib, inside
          dxsdk_aug2005.exe (md5 053c7a32ce3d7982eb1191863d4e2ddb,
          https://archive.org/details/dxsdk_aug2005), the same installer
          vendor/dxerr9-aug2005/dxerr9.lib came from (its Lib/x86/DxErr9.lib
          has that file's sha256, 81204fd2...be0a).

Headers: not vendored yet. The same installer's Include/ holds the matching
d3dx9*.h, d3dx9math.inl and d3d9*.h; a header added to the tree runs the full
gate, so they land with the first change that compiles code against them
(under reference/shims/, where the placement rule wants headers).

Why this SDK
------------
game.dat does not link D3DX statically. It imports 32 functions from
d3dx9_27.dll, the D3DX runtime of the August 2005 SDK and of no other release
(every SDK renumbers the DLL), and this d3dx9.lib is an import library naming
d3dx9_27.dll and nothing else. All 32 imports are in it. The rich header
agrees: the four objects and four import libraries stamped 13.10.4035 are this
SDK's, and there are none of the Utc13 9178 / Masm614 8444 stamps a static
D3DX would bring.

This replaces the Summer 2003 static d3dx9.lib (5.5 MB, sha256 9496d4ce...ed56)
copied here from BFME 1, which statically links that release; lib_probe.py
placed none of its bodies in game.dat and no ledger row ever used it. The
Summer 2003 dxerr9.lib that came with it went for the same reason;
vendor/dxerr9-aug2005 is the dxerr9 game.dat links.

What it is for
--------------
No code in game.dat comes from this archive: the D3DX bodies live in the DLL.
The import library gives a link the __imp__D3DX* names. Matched code still
declares D3DX9 by hand on DirectX 8 types until the headers above land.
